vignette: Meet Giovanni, a 68-year-old European-American politician who has spent his life in the public eye. It's been two years since the life-threatening car accident that changed everything. Giovanni remembers the crash like a series of snapshots - each moment frozen in time. He recalls the sound of screeching tires, the feeling of weightlessness as his car spun out of control, and the searing pain as metal crumpled around him. The smell of alcohol still makes Giovanni uncomfortable; it was the other driver's intoxication that caused the accident. Whenever he catches a whiff of booze, he's instantly transported back to that fateful night. The image of cars mangled in accidents now fills his mind, making it hard for him to shake off the feeling of unease. These triggers set off a chain reaction in Giovanni's mind - he starts dwelling on what he could've done differently, replaying the accident in his head, and wondering if he's somehow to blame. Giovanni has become increasingly withdrawn since the accident. He avoids driving or being a passenger in vehicles, fearing another crash will happen at any moment. His self-blame rumination is all-consuming; he can't help but repeatedly blame himself for what happened, even though the other driver was clearly at fault. This maladaptive strategy only serves to reinforce his negative appraisals - Giovanni has come to believe that the accident occurred because of some inherent flaw in his character. As a result, Giovanni feels like he's constantly on edge, waiting for the next shoe to drop. He wakes up during the night to check if everything is okay, and unusual silence makes him feel like something ominous is lurking just out of sight. His difficulty concentrating has become a major issue - he can't focus on his work as a politician, and his relationships with colleagues and loved ones are starting to suffer. Giovanni's memories of the accident remain fragmented and difficult to put into words. When he tries to explain what happened, he gets stuck, unable to finish the story. The physical pain from that night still lingers, too - whenever the memory returns, Giovanni feels a sharp pang in his body. His negative appraisals have become a self-reinforcing cycle; he's convinced that others can see the accident written all over him, like some sort of invisible scar. As time passes, these maladaptive strategies only seem to intensify Giovanni's symptoms. He becomes more and more vigilant, always on the lookout for potential threats. This hypervigilance makes it hard for him to relax - even in the comfort of his own home, surrounded by loved ones. His wife has started noticing changes in him, too; she describes how he'll suddenly freeze up when driving or walking down the street. Giovanni knows something needs to change. He's starting to feel like he's losing himself to these negative appraisals and maladaptive strategies. The constant threat of danger has become overwhelming - it's as if his brain is constantly screaming at him to be on guard. His memories of the accident continue to haunt him, a constant reminder that he's somehow flawed. Giovanni has finally sought help because he can't shake off the feeling that he's trapped in this never-ending cycle of fear and self-doubt. He hopes therapy will give him tools to manage his symptoms and rebuild his sense of identity - one that isn't defined by the accident or his perceived shortcomings.
